errors.english: [note: seeing the nature of phenomena as being without a permanent self]
errors.why: The opening syllables complete སྒྲིབ་པ་མེད་པ from the previous side, i.e. 'unobstructed', one item in the Śālistamba list; the note invents a different referent.

note: A faithful rendering of the Śālistamba citation and the opening of the MMK closing verse; only the note on the side-initial fragment is wrong.

errors.english: Most people are not attached to the common
errors.why: Dharmakīrti's verse says most people ARE attached to the vulgar/commonplace.

fix.find: Most people are not attached to the common
fix.replace: Most people are attached to the common

errors.english: The water of the eight-limbed river flows along,
errors.why: ཡན་ལག་བརྒྱད་པའི་ཆུ is water of eight qualities (aṣṭāṅga); it flows in rivers, the river is not 'eight-limbed'.

fix.find: The water of the eight-limbed river flows along,
fix.replace: Water of the eight qualities flows in the rivers,

errors.english: and subsequently act for the benefit of others, it will become meaningful
errors.why: The text becomes meaningful because it (the text) accomplishes others' benefit, not because the readers then act for others.

note: Generally sound commentary on the opening of the Bodhicaryāvatāra, but the Dharmakīrti verse has a lost-negation error and the eight-quality water is mistranslated.

errors.english: because they are mistaken [note: they lack the necessary causal sequence]
errors.why: འཁྲུལ་བ here is deviation (vyabhicāra), the opposite of the root verse's མི་འཁྲུལ 'invariable': the horns are not invariably concomitant, not 'mistaken'.

fix.find: because they are mistaken [note: they lack the necessary causal sequence]
fix.replace: because they deviate (are not invariably concomitant) [note: the contrast is with the root verse's 'unerring/invariable']

errors.english: depends upon that very appearance
errors.why: རག here concedes the point ('granted that the knowable appears within consciousness'), setting up the objection; it is not a statement of dependence.

note: Good handling of the Ālambanaparīkṣā argument and the four conditions; the key term 'deviation' in the horns example is mistranslated.

errors.english: if a monk is made to wash items
errors.why: The Tibetan is causative: there is no fault in having someone wash robes soiled by excrement, mud etc.; the ordained person is the one who causes the washing, not the one made to wash.

fix.find: if a monk is made to wash items

errors.english: and the boundaries of the result
errors.why: The earlier ruling referred to is that up to the completion of the result it is a single offence; 'single' (གཅིག་ཉིད) is lost.

errors.english: exchanging the (samghati) outer robe with another monk
errors.why: This is the bhikṣuṇī rule set (the next side concerns other nuns): the offender is a nun exchanging with a monk, so 'another monk' (and 'a monk' as agent elsewhere) misidentifies the subject.

note: The rulings and measures are mostly right, but the commentary is read as addressed to monks when it concerns nuns, and the washing rule's causative is inverted.

errors.english: do not arise dependently [note: in the sense of being real entities]
errors.why: The sentence states the opponent's premise as the first step of a reductio (if the houses were not dependently arisen, neither would grass and wood be), and the author concludes on the next side that they are dependently arisen; the note presents it as the author's own qualified view.

note: Accurate rendering of the gandharva-city, magic and mirage examples; the start of the reply to the objection is slightly misframed.

errors.english: stealing from houses where food is prepared
errors.why: རོ here is 'corpse': a house where corpses are deposited (a charnel house), hence the northern term 'grave-robber'.

fix.find: stealing from houses where food is prepared
fix.replace: stealing from houses where corpses are deposited

errors.english: One who is not overcome by the disease of madness
errors.why: One who IS overcome by the disease of madness is called insane.

fix.find: One who is not overcome by the disease of madness
fix.replace: One who is overcome by the disease of madness

errors.english: One whose thoughts are constantly interrupted and scattered
errors.why: རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པར means uninterruptedly: the distracted person is deranged continuously, in contrast with the madman who intermittently recovers.

note: A Vinaya glossary rendered fluently, but with a lost negation and a misread key word (corpse/taste) that change two definitions.

errors.english: they are explained separately here
errors.why: Because offerings were taught before and rejoicing comes below, the power of the remedy is NOT taught separately here.

fix.replace: they are not explained separately here

errors.english: should it not be explained again here?
errors.why: The objection is that refuge, already explained above, should not be explained here; the English question reads as if it should be.

note: Good on the two kinds of misdeed and the four powers, but the argument why some powers are omitted is inverted at one point.

errors.english: consciousness and the appropriating aggregates are identical
errors.why: ཉེ་བར་ལེན་པ་གཅིག་པ is 'having one material cause' (upādāna), as the following རྒྱུ་གཅིག་པར confirms; the appropriating aggregates are not meant.

fix.find: consciousness and the appropriating aggregates are identical
fix.replace: consciousness and these [pleasure and the rest] have a single material cause

errors.english: the person does grasp the form of pleasure and so forth
errors.why: Because the person would then be subject to transformation, the person does NOT take on the form of pleasure etc.

fix.find: the person does grasp the form of pleasure and so forth
fix.replace: the person does not grasp the form of pleasure and so forth

note: The Sāṃkhya debate is largely followed, but a dropped negation and a misread 'material cause' distort two steps of the argument.

errors.english: Powerful merchant families also mostly do this.
errors.why: དྲག་རིགས is the kṣatriya caste: merchants and kṣatriyas, not 'powerful merchants'.

fix.find: Powerful merchant families also mostly do this.
fix.replace: Merchants and kṣatriyas also mostly do this.

errors.english: I am afflicted
errors.why: The lemma addresses the lustful man: 'you' were tormented over that face, not 'I'.

errors.english: one should generate aversion and think: Why do you not protect it?
errors.why: ཞེ་སྡང is anger: the point is that the lover, who grew angry when others looked at her, does not protect the body when vultures eat it; 'aversion' turns this into disgust toward the body.

note: Serviceable gloss commentary on Bodhicaryāvatāra 8, with a caste term and the addressee of one lemma wrong.

errors.english: between the positions of those who rely [note: on external objects] and those who do not
errors.why: The edition note marks བརྟེན for བརྟན: the debate (previous side, and later on this side) is between the positions that things are stable and that they are momentary.

fix.find: between the positions of those who rely [note: on external objects] and those who do not
fix.replace: between the positions that things are stable and that they are not (momentary)

errors.english: the opponent's position is challenged on both sides
errors.why: It is the opponent who raises an objection against both positions (with and without aspect); the author then answers that the objection applies to both parties.

fix.find: the opponent's position is challenged on both sides
fix.replace: the opponent raises an objection against both positions

note: The sākāra/anākāra argument is followed well, but the stable/momentary framing is misread at the start and the objector is misidentified.
